323.title: The second generation
323.hook: children grow up with Punjabi at home, other languages outside, and Gurmukhi classes at weekends
323.howItsDone: Many gurdwaras outside India run weekend Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes, kirtan lessons and youth camps so children can read the Guru Granth Sahib and feel at home in both worlds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar: rice, dal and tea at borders and floods, and your line, the kitchen travels. Today, the kids who grew up eating that langar, far from Punjab.

Saturday morning, a gurdwara in Toronto, or Leicester, or Melbourne, or California. In a side room, a dozen kids sit at folding tables with notebooks, tracing curly letters while a patient teacher says each sound out loud. They'd rather be asleep, or at soccer. At home they speak Punjabi with their grandparents, English with their siblings, and something in between with their parents. At school, someone asks about the patka on a boy's head for the hundredth time.
screen: `SATURDAY MORNING, A SIDE ROOM.` → `TRACING CURLY LETTERS.` → `PUNJABI AT HOME, ENGLISH OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: The children of Sikh immigrants grow up in two worlds at once. At home: Punjabi, parathas, the Guru Granth Sahib in the front room or a picture of the Gurus on the wall, early morning prayers played from a phone. Outside: school, friends, sports, a whole other language and way of doing things. Some switch between them without a second thought. Some say they feel pulled in two directions. Some cut their hair as teenagers, and some of those grow it back later. Some take amrit young. Plenty are still working it out. That's why the weekend Gurmukhi class carries so much weight. Gurmukhi is the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, and its name is usually explained as from the mouth of the Guru. Tradition says the second Guru, Guru Angad, shaped and spread it, and taught children to read, so ordinary people could read the Guru's words for themselves. So the kids tracing letters in Toronto are repeating a lesson tradition says Guru Angad gave the children around him. It's not just a language lesson. It's a key to the Guru. And the second generation has given something back: Sikh camps, youth groups, podcasts and videos, and a way of explaining the turban, the langar and the Gurus to classmates in the language of the playground. They carry two worlds. The hope of the weekend class is one heart underneath: the same Guru, the same sangat, just speaking more than one language.

segments.voice: Choose a word from a language that isn't your main one: one you learned on this path, like sangat or seva, or one a friend or your grandparents taught you. Say it quietly, and notice how it sits in your mouth, whatever that turns out to be. Then think of someone who lives between two languages every day, and hold them kindly.
Gurmukhi. The script of the Guru Granth Sahib — taught on weekends to the second generation, children of Sikh immigrants who grow up with Punjabi at home and other languages outside.
Your line: two worlds, one heart. Saturday's curly letters open the Guru's words. Day three hundred twenty-three, done.

324.title: Kirtan in new places
324.hook: hymns now sound in gurdwaras on every continent, in old ragas and new voices
324.howItsDone: Kirtan is sung in gurdwaras, usually with harmonium and tabla and sometimes with stringed instruments; the kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast daily for Sikhs around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi: Saturday classes, Punjabi at home, and your line, two worlds, one heart. Today, the thing that sounds the same in both worlds: the Guru's song.

Before dawn in Amritsar, the kirtan at the Harmandir Sahib has already begun. In Kuala Lumpur, a few hours ahead, a group of old men in a gurdwara is singing along with a tabla. In Nairobi, a family will sing at its own sunrise, a few hours later. And in Vancouver, still the afternoon before, a teenager practices on a harmonium with headphones on so she won't bother her little brother. Follow the clock around the planet, and the same hymns keep turning up.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN IN AMRITSAR.` → `KUALA LUMPUR, NAIROBI, VANCOUVER.` → `THE SAME HYMNS KEEP TURNING UP.`

segments.voice: Kirtan means singing the praise of God, and for Sikhs it means singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib. It began with Guru Nanak and his companion Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician who played the rabab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the start, the Guru's word was meant to be sung. That's why the main body of the Guru Granth Sahib is divided first by raag, musical modes, each with its own mood and time of day, and only then, inside each raag, by author and form. There are thirty-one main raags: some belong to dawn, some to evening, some to longing, some to joy. Over the centuries, the instruments changed. The harmonium came to India with Europeans in the 1800s and became a familiar sound in gurdwaras. In recent decades, some musicians have gone back to the older strings: the rabab, the dilruba, the taus. So kirtan today is both: old raags and new voices. The diaspora has carried it a long way, to gurdwaras across the world, classrooms and camps, phones and livestreams. The kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast every day, so a grandmother in England can listen along with Amritsar at breakfast. Children learn the tabla in the same gurdwaras where their parents learned to read Gurmukhi. And some listeners who aren't Sikh say they were drawn in before they understood a word. The Gurus taught that the Name is sung, not only studied. Now that song turns up everywhere.

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of kirtan, or the live broadcast from the Harmandir Sahib, softly; if you can't right now, remember any kirtan you've heard on this path. Don't try to follow the words: let the sound come to you from far away, the way it reaches homes on the other side of the world. When your mind wanders, come back to the sound.
Kirtan. Singing the Guru's hymns — in old raags and new voices, it now sounds in gurdwaras and homes across the world.
Your line: the song everywhere. Somewhere on earth, right now, someone is singing the Guru's hymns. See you tomorrow.

325.title: No stranger anywhere
325.hook: no one is my enemy and no one a stranger; I get along with all (Kanara, ang 1299)
325.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's hymn in Raag Kanara (Ang 1299) in kirtan, and many quote its line 'na ko bairi nahi bigana' as a summary of how the Gurus asked them to see others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: old raags, new voices, and your line, the song everywhere. Today, one line from that song the whole diaspora could have written on its suitcases.

The first day in a new place. A new school, a new job, a new country. Everyone else knows where the bathrooms are and who sits with whom. You're the stranger. Now the other side: the day a stranger walks into your place, and you have to decide whether to smile. For two weeks this path has followed Sikhs who were strangers almost everywhere they went: Hong Kong, Vancouver, Stockton, Southall. Today, a line from Guru Arjan turns the whole idea of stranger inside out.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY IN A NEW PLACE.` → `WHETHER TO SMILE.` → `A LINE FROM GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: The hymn is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in Raag Kanara, on page one thousand two hundred ninety-nine of the Guru Granth Sahib. It begins with a confession: I've forgotten all my envy of others, since I found the company of the holy. Then comes the line: Na ko bairi nahi bigana, sagal sang ham kau ban aai. No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone. Bairi is an enemy. Bigana is a stranger, an outsider, someone who isn't one of us. And the Guru says there aren't any. Not because everyone is nice, but because of what comes next in the hymn: the one God is present in everyone, and seeing that, again and again, Nanak blossoms. If the same light is in every face, nobody is a stranger, just someone you haven't met. Notice where this way of seeing comes from: the sangat. The Guru says it arrived with holy company. You don't get there alone, by thinking; you get there by sitting with people. That's what the diaspora did. They came as strangers to Malaya and Canada and California and Britain. They were turned away from harbors, refused citizenship, told to take off their turbans, attacked. And again and again they opened a room, installed the Guru, cooked langar, and fed whoever walked in, including the people who had treated them as strangers. That closes this path's look at the diaspora, from leaving Punjab to kitchens at every border.

segments.voice: Picture someone you'll probably see today but don't know: a cashier, a bus driver, a new face at work, someone on your street, and see their face as clearly as you can. Now picture greeting them the way you'd greet a cousin you haven't seen in a while: a real smile, their name if you know it. Notice what shifts in you.
Bigana. A stranger or outsider — na ko bairi nahi bigana: no one is my enemy and no one a stranger; I get along with all.
Your line: no one is a stranger. That's day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: Looking back: the stories
326.hook: ten Gurus, the sakhis, the Khalsa's birth: which story stayed with you
326.howItsDone: Sikh families tell sakhis, stories of the Gurus, to children at home and in gurdwara classes, and katha (explanation) in the gurdwara often retells a sakhi alongside the day's hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bigana: Guru Arjan's line, no enemy and no stranger, and your line, no one is a stranger. Today, a look back from the year's lookout.

What have you actually learned on this path? Someone will ask at dinner one day. You could list facts, or tell a story. A man who walked into a river and didn't come out for three days. A carpenter's plain bread, and a rich man's feast. A boy who told his father, no one is more worthy than you. A sword drawn before a crowd, and five people who stood up. A faith often travels in its stories more than its facts. This week looks back at the whole year, starting with them.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU LEARNED?` → `A RIVER, A LOAF, A SWORD.` → `THE STORIES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Camp two's stories came in a line of ten Gurus. Guru Nanak, three days in the river Bein, coming out to say there is no Hindu and no Muslim. Eating Bhai Lalo's honest bread and refusing Malik Bhago's feast. Walking the world with Mardana and his rabab, then farming at Kartarpur. Guru Angad shaping the Gurmukhi letters, while Mata Khivi ran the kitchen. Guru Amar Das, the old man who carried water before dawn and who, the story goes, asked everyone, even an emperor, to eat in the langar first. Guru Ram Das digging the pool at Amritsar. Guru Arjan building a temple with four doors and gathering the hymns into one book, then dying in custody in Lahore, remembered by Sikhs as a martyr. Guru Hargobind wearing two swords. Guru Har Rai and his herb garden. Guru Har Krishan, a child nursing the sick in Delhi. Guru Tegh Bahadur giving his life for the freedom of people of another faith. And Guru Gobind Singh: Vaisakhi, 1699, the sword, the five beloved, sugar stirred into water in an iron bowl, and the Guru asking the five to initiate him. Then, in 1708, the Guruship passing to the Granth. A story of the Gurus is a sakhi, a word usually traced to an old word for a witness. A good sakhi doesn't just inform you. It stands beside you as a witness when you need it: at a table where someone's being left out, at a moment you want to cheat, on a day you need courage. The question isn't which story matters most, but which one stayed with you.
screen: `TEN GURUS, ONE LINE.` · `NANAK TO GOBIND SINGH.` · `THE GURU BECOMES THE GRANTH.` · `A SAKHI IS A WITNESS.` · then, large: `WHICH STORY STAYED?`

segments.voice: Let the stories drift past; wait for the one that tugs at you, not the one you think you should pick. Tell it softly in your own words, out loud if you can, as if to a child; it's fine to forget details, just tell what happened and why it matters to you. Then sit with it in the quiet.
Looking back. The year's stories: ten Gurus, the sakhis, the Khalsa's birth, and the one that stayed with you.
Your line: which story stayed. A sakhi stands beside you. Until tomorrow.

327.title: Looking back: the practices
327.hook: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem and the gurdwara: which one you kept
327.howItsDone: Sikhs weave seva, kirtan, langar, simran and Nitnem into ordinary days and gather at the gurdwara; many describe Guru Nanak's three pillars, naam japna, kirat karni and vand chhakna, as the frame that holds them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the stories: ten Gurus, the sakhis, and your line, which story stayed. Today, a look back at what you did with your hands and breath.

New Year's resolutions get announced. The habits that actually last tend to sneak in quietly. A walk after dinner. A song hummed while washing up. A particular way of saying goodnight. Nobody forced them; they just fit. Camp three opened a whole toolbox of Sikh practices, one after another. Nobody keeps every tool in daily use. One or two get picked up again and again, and those become yours.
screen: `THE HABITS THAT JUST STUCK.` → `A WHOLE TOOLBOX.` → `ONE OR TWO BECOME YOURS.`

segments.voice: Open the toolbox. Seva: service with no audience. Minding shoes at the gurdwara door, washing a dish slowly, setting aside a tenth, teaching someone kindly. And the warning that came with it: when seva feeds the ego, it stops being seva. Kirtan: first just listening, then humming, then singing Waheguru to a simple tune, then one line, the rahao, the pause line that holds a hymn's center. Langar: sitting level on the floor in rows, rolling rotis, receiving with cupped hands, and feeding one person at home with no agenda. Simran: remembering the Name on the breath, Wahe on the in-breath, Guru on the out-breath, in the early hours before dawn, and the mind running off, again and again, and the practice being only to come back. Nitnem: the daily banis, Japji at dawn, Rehras at dusk, Kirtan Sohila at night, and the reminder that a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test. And the gurdwara: covering your head, taking off your shoes, bowing to the Word, the warm karah prashad in your hands, the hukamnama read from the page where the Granth is opened. In Sikh teaching these aren't separate hobbies. They're one life: the Guru's word sung, remembered, served and shared. Sikhs often sum up Guru Nanak's teaching in three pillars: remember the Name, earn honestly, share what you have. But a path is walked one step at a time, and one practice can become a door to the others. So which one stuck for you? Not which one should have. Which one did?

segments.voice: If it was simran, breathe Wahe in, Guru out; if kirtan, hum a line you remember; if Nitnem, say the first line you know. If it was seva or langar, picture the task you'll do later and do it now in your mind, slowly and well; if nothing stuck yet, just breathe and let one of them choose you. Whatever it is, give it the whole two minutes.
Looking back. The year's practices: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem and the gurdwara, and the one that became yours.
Your line: the practice that stuck. One door can open the others. That's three hundred twenty-seven.

328.title: Looking back: the Japji
328.hook: thirty-eight pauris heard and understood, one by one
328.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the Japji every morning as the first of the daily banis, from memory or from a gutka, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the practices: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem, and your line, the practice that stuck. Today, the climb through one text: the Japji.

A whole scripture, read slowly, line by line: sound first, meaning second. That was camp four. Day after day it walked through Guru Nanak's Japji, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib and the first bani of a Sikh morning. Each day began with a line said aloud in Gurmukhi, tongue-twisters and all. Then came what it meant. Somewhere in the middle, it may have stopped feeling like homework.
screen: `A WHOLE SCRIPTURE, SLOWLY.` → `SOUND FIRST, MEANING SECOND.` → `CAMP FOUR: THE JAPJI.`

segments.voice: It began before the first pauri, with the Mool Mantar: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one Creator, whose name is truth, without fear, without hate, beyond time, never born, self-existent, known by the Guru's grace. Then the salok: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true forever. Then pauri one, and its first line, said aloud back in camp four: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar. Thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there. The way through is hukam, walking in the order. Pauri two: everything comes by that order, and whoever understands it stops saying I, I. Then the great runs. Suniai: by listening. Mannai: by trusting. Asankh: countless prayers and countless fools, and Nanak calling himself too small to count them. Then the realms, one after another, like a ladder: duty, knowledge, effort, grace, and at the top, the realm of truth, where the Formless dwells. Pauri thirty-eight, the mint: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Let restraint be the furnace and patience the goldsmith, and there the Word is minted. And last, the salok that closes it: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. From thinking you can't get there, to seeing the whole world as your family: that's the arc of the Japji. If you walked those days with it, you've earned a plain sentence: I read it. Not mastered, not memorized. Read, one pauri at a time.

segments.voice: Which pauri stayed with you: the first one, about overthinking, listening, the countless, the mint? If you can, find it and read it slowly, the Gurmukhi sound if you can manage it, then the meaning; if you can't look it up now, say what you remember of it. Then sit with it, and let it be yours for a while.

329.title: Looking back: the depths
329.hook: themes, Bhagats, rehat, history and grief carried carefully
329.howItsDone: Sikhs deepen their understanding through katha (explanation of the hymns), study of the Guru Granth Sahib and Sikh history, and remembrance of the panth's struggles in the daily Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the Japji: from sochai soch to air, water and earth, and your line, I read it. Today, the last and deepest stretch of the year: camp five, the depths.

There's a point, swimming out from a beach, where your feet reach down and find nothing. The water gets darker and colder. Then, with a steady breath, something changes. The water holds you up. The shore behind you looks small. Camp five was that kind of water. A hundred days past where the feet can touch: the Granth's biggest ideas, the Bhagats, the Sikh way of life, centuries of history, and a week of real grief.
screen: `PAST WHERE YOUR FEET TOUCH.` → `DARKER, COLDER, THEN HELD UP.` → `A HUNDRED DAYS OF DEEP WATER.`

segments.voice: It began with the shape of the Guru Granth Sahib: fourteen hundred thirty pages, each called an ang, a limb; many voices, one Guru. Then the great themes: hukam, the order; haumai, the ego that is its own disease and holds its own cure; naam, the Name; nadar, the kindly glance of grace. The five thieves in the house of the mind, and the five virtues that guard it. The Guru asking why woman should be called lesser, when kings are born of her. Asking about the light in a person, not their caste. Then the Bhagats: Kabir the weaver and Farid the Sufi, whose hymns the Gurus kept beside their own. Then rehat, the Sikh way of life: kesh, kangha, kara, kachhera and kirpan, amrit, the written code, the many ways of being Sikh, the saint-soldier. Then the long history: Banda Singh, the years in the forests, the two ghallugharas, Ranjit Singh covering the Harmandir Sahib in gold, annexation, Jallianwala Bagh, the peaceful struggle for the gurdwaras, Partition, and a door opening at Kartarpur. Then 1984, carried as carefully as this path could. And the diaspora, strangers who became neighbors everywhere. The Guru Granth Sahib often pictures the world as a vast, frightening ocean, the bhavjal, and the Guru's word as the boat that carries you across. That's a fair picture of camp five. Some of it was beautiful and wide open. Some of it was dark and cold and hard to look at. Nobody had to understand all of it to get across. The way over was a day at a time, with the Guru's word as the boat.
screen: `THE GRANTH'S SHAPE AND THEMES.` · `THE BHAGATS AND THE REHAT.` · `HISTORY, AND GRIEF CARRIED.` · `THE BOAT ACROSS THE OCEAN.` · then, large: `DEEP WATER, CROSSED.`

segments.voice: Let one hard part of this year's path come back to you: a teaching that challenged you, a story that hurt to hear, a question you still can't answer. Don't try to fix it or solve it; let it sit beside you like a companion on a long swim, and notice that you're still here, still breathing, held up. Then let it rest.
Looking back. Camp five, the depths: the Granth's themes, the Bhagats, rehat, history, and grief carried carefully.
Your line: deep water, crossed. This year, you've already crossed it, one day at a time. See you tomorrow.
